Jim Cramer: Amazon Could Sell Its Anthropic Stake and Say "Our CapEx Is Paid For." Does the Math Work? © Viktoryia Vinnikava's Images and Tiger Lily from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Jim Cramer said Amazon could sell its Anthropic stake and have its capex "paid for for the next year and a half."

The Anthropic shares Amazon owns outright were worth about $188 billion at the first-day close, about 10 months of this year's capex.

Amazon only needs to cover its free cash flow shortfall, about $65 billion across 2026 and 2027, and those shares cover it more than twice over.

Andy Jassy says Amazon will hold the stake. It's a backstop, and its value, like Salesforce's, now moves with Anthropic's stock.

Anthropic's IPO made Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) one of the market's biggest winners on paper, and Jim Cramer has an idea for what to do with the winnings.

Anthropic (ANT:NASDAQ) closed its first day of trading Thursday at $97.17, 17% above its $83 IPO price, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday as AI stocks sold off. On Squawk on the Street, CNBC's Cramer laid out the math:

"that number of their ownership in Anthropic is more than equivalent to what they're going to spend in CapEx. They could actually sell the stake and say, hey, our CapEx is paid for for the next year and a half."

That would be quite the trick. CEO Andy Jassy told CNBC's Halftime Report on Nov. 17 that "we expect to spend around $220 billion this year in CapEx and that we expect to spend meaningfully more next year."

Free cash flow has gone negative

That spending has already pushed Amazon's free cash flow below zero. Analysts don't expect it to turn positive again until 2028:

Amazon (AMZN): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

So far, Amazon has filled the gap mostly by borrowing. Its long-term debt rose from $65.6 billion at the end of 2025 to $173.1 billion at Sept. 30, more than doubling in nine months.

TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Amazon. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Amazon, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Amazon's Analyst Ratings

Cramer counts the notes

After the IPO, Amazon owns 14.6% of Anthropic outright. At the first-day close, those shares were worth about $188 billion, roughly 10 months of this year's capex.

Cramer's figure is 23.6%, because it also counts convertible notes Amazon hasn't converted, held back under an ownership cap it has chosen not to waive. At the $1.5 trillion valuation he used, that's about $354 billion, or about 19 months of spending at this year's pace.

But Amazon's capex has more than doubled in five years:

Amazon (AMZN): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Analysts expect $278.2 billion in 2027, and at that pace even Cramer's $354 billion covers only about 15 months.

Salesforce vs. ServiceNow: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool

CRM
NOW
BRZE
MSFT

Trading disclosure

The shift toward enterprise automation and artificial intelligence has created a fierce battle between two cloud software titans. Investors choosing between Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) must decide which platform offers better value.

Salesforce dominates the customer relationship management space, helping businesses track every client interaction. ServiceNow specializes in streamlining back-office workflows, from IT support to HR tasks. Both companies are now racing to integrate generative AI into their ecosystems, making this a pivotal comparison for investors seeking growth in tech stocks.

The case for Salesforce

Salesforce provides cloud-based software that connects sales, marketing, and IT on a single platform to serve over 150,000 companies. It has recently prioritized AI integration through a major partnership with Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) for "Copilotforce," which combines customer context with AI experiences. The company continues expanding its reach through acquisitions such as Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE) to deepen engagement. Salesforce serves businesses of all sizes globally, and no single customer accounts for more than 10% of its total revenue.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached approximately $43.9 billion, representing growth of nearly 11.2% over the prior period. The company also generated net income of roughly $9.7 billion, which reflects a net margin of close to 22%. This growth trend has been supported by a steady increase in revenue from $34.9 billion just two years ago. The business focuses on maintaining profitability while scaling its cloud ecosystem and proprietary AI tools.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.3x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio, a measure of how well a company covers short-term debts with short-term assets, is approximately 0.8x. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $14.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for ServiceNow

ServiceNow offers an AI platform designed to automate enterprise work across departments including IT, human resources, and finance. The company focuses on large enterprise clients, ending recent periods with over 600 customers spending more than $5 million annually. It maintains strategic partnerships with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Accenture (NYSE:ACN) to drive AI-driven workflow integrations for its 8,700 total customers. This strategy targets a growing presence in the public sector and large organizations seeking efficient digital transformation.

Salesforce (CRM) is facing another round of job cuts just as investors are already questioning the sustainability of its growth in an increasingly artificial intelligence (AI) -driven software market. According to reports, Salesforce has begun another workforce reduction, with employees discussing layoffs in internal Slack channels and a senior manager confirming that they and several colleagues were affected. The company has not disclosed the size or scope of the latest cuts.

The latest reductions add to a series of workforce cuts this year, including layoffs impacting hundreds of positions across California, Washington, and other markets. Salesforce also cut fewer than 1,000 roles earlier in 2026, including positions in marketing, product management, data analytics, and its Agentforce AI business.

Salesforce (CRM) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.

Over the past month, shares of this customer-management software developer have returned -26.8%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -6.6% change. During this period, the Zacks Internet - Software industry, which Salesforce falls in, has lost 13.3%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

For the current quarter, Salesforce is expected to post earnings of $3.43 per share, indicating a change of +5.5% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged over the last 30 days.

The consensus earnings estimate of $16.72 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +33.6%. This estimate has remained unchanged over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $16.03 indicates a change of -4.1% from what Salesforce is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) for Salesforce.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

$1 million put into Microsoft at the Friday, Nov 18, 2016 close was worth about $9.25 million at Thursday's close. That counts dividends put back into the stock. That is more than nine times the money. On price alone, the stake came to $8,256,835.

The ride was harder than that end number suggests. Microsoft's worst fall in the ten years was 37.6%. It ran from Nov 19, 2021 to Nov 3, 2022. Counting from the Nov 19, 2021 peak, the stock took 573 days to close above it again. Its most recent big fall, 34.9% to June 25, 2026, came close to that worst one.

Is Microsoft the big tech stock best placed to ride out an AI slowdown? This article looks at the ride first. It asks how far Microsoft fell and how long it took to heal, against Nvidia and Amazon. The question is timely. Stocks fell broadly on Thursday. Microsoft closed down 2.0% at $498.30.

How bad was Microsoft's worst fall?

Microsoft closed at $343.11 on Nov 19, 2021. It hit a low of $214.25 on Nov 3, 2022. The fall lasted 349 days, and the climb back took another 224 days. The stock first closed above its old peak on June 15, 2023, at $348.10. This article does not try to say what caused this fall or the others.

Microsoft dropped 37.6% and needed 573 days from its peak to get back above it. If Microsoft is a big part of your savings, that is a long drop to sit through and a long wait just to get even. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.

That was not the only deep fall. Microsoft fell 20% or more four times in the ten years. We count a fall from a record close to the lowest close before the stock gets back to that record. Here are all four:

Feb 10 to Mar 16, 2020: down 28.2%, back above the peak 120 days after it.

Nov 19, 2021 to Nov 3, 2022: down 37.6%, back above the peak 573 days after it.

Jul 5, 2024 to Apr 8, 2025: down 24.2%, back above the peak 335 days after it.

Oct 28, 2025 to Jun 25, 2026: down 34.9%, back above the peak 350 days after it.

All four had healed by Thursday's close. Microsoft set a new record close of $555.80 on Nov 4, 2026. At Thursday's close it was 10.3% below that record.
